unit.title: Prepare and present appetizers and salads

summary: This unit teaches you to prepare and present appetisers and salads for villa guests, receptions and buffets: the food safety rules for cold, ready-to-eat food, canapés and other appetisers (cold and hot), Jamaican favourites such as Solomon Gundy, stamp and go and pepper shrimp, green, simple and compound salads, dressings such as vinaigrette and mayonnaise, allergens, and neat, safe presentation and display.

blocks.p: Appetisers and salads are the first food a guest sees, so they set the tone for the meal. They also carry the highest food safety risk in the kitchen, because most of them are **eaten without any more cooking**. A pan of chicken is made safe by the heat of the stove. A salad is made safe only by clean hands, clean produce, cold storage and careful handling. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

Villa and hotel guests expect fresh, colourful, neatly presented food, and many of them love local flavours such as saltfish fritters, pepper shrimp and bammy. Many also have allergies or follow special diets. So this unit is about **safety, freshness, neat work and careful labelling**.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's kitchen: canapés and a hot appetiser for a reception, and a salad bar with dressings and a chilled display. The assessor watches your hygiene, temperatures, neatness, labelling and teamwork.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Food safety for cold and ready-to-eat food

blocks.h: Why salads and cold appetisers are high risk

ul: They are **ready-to-eat**: nobody cooks them again, so any bacteria that reach them stay alive until the guest eats them.
Many contain high-risk foods: cooked chicken, seafood, eggs, cooked rice or potatoes, and mayonnaise.
They are handled a lot: cut, mixed, arranged and put on plates.
In Jamaica's heat, bacteria multiply quickly once food warms up.

blocks.h: Personal hygiene at the salad station

head: Habit
Why
rows: Wash your hands before you start, after raw food, after the toilet, after touching your face, hair or phone, and between tasks
Hands are the main route for germs into ready-to-eat food.
Prevents hair and dirt falling into the food.
Short, clean, unpolished nails; no false nails; no rings (except a plain band), watches or bracelets
Nail polish can chip into food, and jewellery hides dirt and can fall in.
Waterproof, **blue** plasters on cuts, with a glove over them
Blue is not a colour of food, so a plaster that falls into food is easy to see.
Do not prepare food if you have vomiting, diarrhoea or an infected sore, and tell your supervisor
You can pass the illness to guests.
Required for every food handler in Jamaica. It is issued through the local public health department.

ul: Use **clean tongs, spoons or clean disposable gloves**. Do not touch ready-to-eat food with bare hands.
Wash your hands before putting on gloves. Gloves are not a substitute for washing; change them when they are torn, when you change task, after touching raw food, your face, a bin, money or a phone.
Use separate boards and knives. In a common colour code, **green** is for salad and fruit and red for raw meat. Follow the Centre's code.
Wash and dry all fruit and vegetables, including those you will peel. Germs on the skin of melon or pineapple travel on the knife to the flesh.
Taste with a clean spoon each time. Never taste with your finger.
Store raw meat and seafood away from salad, on the bottom shelf of the fridge.

head: Food
Temperature (or as the Centre's food safety plan says)
rows: Salads, cold appetisers, dressings with egg, cut fruit
Hot appetisers (patties, fritters, skewers) held for service
Cooked chicken or other poultry in a skewer or filling
Cooked to a core temperature of about **74 °C**.
Cooked items used in cold dishes (potatoes, eggs, rice, chicken)
Cool quickly and chill before mixing with other items.

blocks.p: Between 5 °C and 63 °C is the **danger zone**, where bacteria grow fastest. Take only as much food out of the fridge as you can use at a time, and put the rest back.

Cold food on a buffet must stay at 5 °C or below on ice or in a chilled unit. Food that has been out for longer than the Centre's food safety plan allows (commonly 2 to 4 hours in total) must be **thrown away**, not put back in the fridge. Write down the time food is put out.

An **allergen** is something in food that can cause a harmful reaction in some people. The most common are peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, wheat and gluten, soya and sesame. Some reactions are severe and can kill.

head: Guest
Check for
Examples
rows: Peanuts and tree nuts (walnuts in Waldorf salad, nuts in dressings and pesto)
Waldorf salad, some dressings, some biscuits
Egg in mayonnaise, creamy dressings and Caesar dressing, quiche, egg salad, some breads and batters
Cream cheese, butter, cream, cheese, yoghurt dressings
Canapés spread with cream cheese; Caesar with parmesan
Shrimp, lobster, crab, fish; fish hidden in sauces such as Worcestershire sauce and some Caesar dressings (anchovy)
Shrimp cocktail, pepper shrimp, Solomon Gundy
Bread, crackers, croutons, batter, some sauces
Canapé bases, croutons, stamp and go fritters
Meat, fish, gelatine; vegans also avoid egg, milk, honey
Mayonnaise, cream cheese; salads can be made vegan with oil dressings

ul: Ask about allergies and special diets when the order is taken. Write them on the order and tell the head cook.
Read **every** label, including dressings, sauces, crackers and bread.
Use clean utensils and a clean board for an allergy dish. Keep it covered and labelled. A shared spoon or a crumb can be enough to cause a reaction.
Label every dish on a buffet with its name and the allergens.
If you are not sure, say so and ask the chef. Never guess.

head: Name
What it is
Example
rows: A small dish served to start a meal and wake up the appetite.
A small shrimp cocktail; callaloo fritters.
French term for small appetisers served before a meal, often passed round on a tray.
A small bite on a base (bread, toast, cracker, pastry or bammy round) with a spread, a topping and a garnish, eaten in one or two bites, often standing.
Solomon Gundy on a cracker; smoked marlin on cucumber.
Any small food eaten with the fingers.
Served chilled or at room temperature.
Stamp and go; mini patties; jerk skewers.
Raw vegetable sticks served with a dip.
Carrot, cucumber and sweet pepper with a dip.
A tiny free bite chosen by the chef at the start of a fine-dining meal.

head: Appetiser
What it is
Notes
rows: A spicy spread made from pickled or smoked herring (or similar fish), hot pepper, pimento, onion and vinegar.
Served on crackers, bammy or toast. Contains fish; the crackers contain wheat.
Fried saltfish fritters: flaked saltfish in a flour batter with onion, escallion, thyme and a little pepper.
Soak or boil the saltfish to take out the salt. Keep hot at 63 °C or above for a reception.
Shrimp boiled in a spicy, peppery stock with pimento and scotch bonnet. Famous from Middle Quarters, St Elizabeth, where it is sold along the road.
Allergen: shellfish. Very hot; warn guests.
Rounds of bammy (cassava flatbread), fried or steamed, with a topping.
Cassava, so no wheat, but check the label.
Thin, crisp slices of green plantain, fried and salted.
Small pastry pies with a spiced filling.
Allergens: wheat, and maybe egg and milk. Keep hot.
Callaloo and cream cheese on bammy
Cooked, cooled callaloo with cream cheese.
Jerk-seasoned chicken pieces on small sticks.

blocks.note: Pepper shrimp and stamp and go are best bought or cooked fresh. Shrimp is a high-risk food: keep it at 5 °C or below and make sure it is cooked through and then chilled quickly.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Part
What it is
Notes
rows: Toast, cracker, bread round, pastry case, bammy, cucumber slice.
Crisp, firm and a size for one or two bites.
Butter, cream cheese or a thick spread, put on the base right to the edge.
Stops moisture from the topping soaking into the base so it goes soggy.
Solomon Gundy, smoked marlin, shrimp, callaloo, cheese, chicken.
Keep chilled until it is used. Cut to a neat, even size.
A small, edible item: herb sprig, a slice of sweet pepper, a twist of lime.
Must suit the flavour; do not use non-edible items.

flow: Work out the numbers and the types, using a mix of colours, flavours and textures
Prepare the parts in advance: bake or toast the bases, make the spreads, cook and chill the toppings, cut the garnish
Keep the toppings and spreads in the fridge until just before assembly
Assemble on a clean, green (salad) board, using clean tongs or gloves, close to service time so that the base stays crisp
Make every piece the same size and shape
Arrange on a chilled or clean platter, covered until service, with allergens labelled
Replenish from the fridge in small batches

ul: **Amounts:** for a reception before a meal, a common guide is 4 to 6 pieces per guest; for a reception that replaces a meal, 10 to 12 or more. Check the order. Example: 40 guests with 3 cold and 2 hot pieces each need 120 cold and 80 hot pieces. If there are three kinds of cold canapé, make 40 of each.
**Size:** one or two bites, so guests can eat while standing, holding a drink.
**Odd numbers** (3, 5, 7) of items in a group often look more pleasing than even numbers.
**Variety:** a mix of fish, meat, vegetable and cheese; hot and cold; mild and spicy.
Prepare cold canapés last, and do not leave them out longer than the plan allows.

blocks.note: Sweet and spicy flavours are popular with guests, but scotch bonnet pepper is very hot. Tell guests when something is very spicy, and use gloves when you handle the pepper. Wash your hands, board and knife afterwards.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A classic **shrimp (prawn) cocktail** is cooked, cooled shrimp, served chilled on shredded lettuce in a glass or small dish, with a pink sauce (**Marie Rose**: mayonnaise mixed with tomato ketchup and a few drops of lemon or lime juice and pepper sauce). Garnish with a wedge of lime. Keep the dish on crushed ice on a buffet.

head: Leaf
Character
Use
rows: Green salads, sandwiches; dress at the last minute.
Spinach, pak choi, callaloo leaves (raw young leaves)

flow: Wash your hands; clean the sink or use clean bowls
Remove damaged outer leaves and cut off roots and stems
Separate the leaves and wash in plenty of cold, clean water, lifting them out, not draining the dirty water over them
Change the water and repeat until no soil or sand is left
Dry well in a salad spinner, or on clean cloths or paper
Store covered in the fridge, at 5 °C or below

ul: **Dry leaves well**: water left on the leaves dilutes and slides off the dressing, and wet leaves go soft and slimy.
A **salad spinner** dries leaves quickly by spinning the water off.
**Tear lettuce by hand** rather than cutting with a knife if you can, because cut edges turn brown more quickly. Cutting with a clean stainless steel knife is acceptable when speed matters.
Wash all vegetables and fruit, even if they will be peeled.

head: Cut
What it looks like
Use
rows: Potato, beetroot, cucumber for compound salads.

ul: Cut pieces to the same size so the salad looks neat and tastes even.
Use a sharp knife on a steady board with a damp cloth under it. Curl the fingers of your guiding hand.
A **mandoline** slices very evenly, but it is sharp: use the hand guard or a cut-resistant glove.
A **grater** is used for carrot and cabbage; guard your knuckles and stop before the last piece gets small.
A **melon baller** scoops round balls from melon or pawpaw.
Choose **firm, ripe tomatoes** with a good red colour. Soft, over-ripe ones go watery.
Cucumber can be peeled or left with its skin on; dry the slices so they do not water down the salad.
**Avocado (pear)** goes brown when cut because it reacts with air. Squeeze lime juice on the cut flesh and cover it. Prepare it close to service.
**Fresh fruit salad** stays fresh if you cut it as late as possible, cover it and chill it. Add lime juice to apples, bananas and pawpaw to slow browning. Soft fruit such as banana is added last.

sections.title: Salads: kinds, parts and classic dishes

blocks.p: A **simple salad** is made of one main item, or one type of item, and a dressing: a tomato salad, a cucumber salad, a green salad of lettuce. A **compound (mixed) salad** is made of several items mixed or arranged together, usually with a richer dressing: potato salad, coleslaw, Caesar salad, a chicken salad.

blocks.h: The four parts of a plated salad

head: Part
What it is
Example
rows: The bed of leaves or other food on which the salad sits.
The main part of the salad.
Sliced tomato and cucumber; chicken; shrimp.
The sauce that adds flavour and moisture.
A sprig of parsley, a slice of lime, a few cherry tomatoes.

head: Salad
Main ingredients
Notes
rows: Lettuce, cucumber, tomato, carrot, sweet pepper, onion
Shredded cabbage and carrot, with mayonnaise or a vinaigrette
Salt draws water out of the cabbage, so mix it late. Keep chilled.
Diced Irish potato, diced boiled beetroot (which turns it pink), hard-boiled egg, onion, sweet pepper, mayonnaise
Cool the potatoes and eggs first. High risk: keep at 5 °C or below. Allergens: egg.
Cos lettuce, croutons, parmesan cheese and a creamy dressing
Dressing may contain egg and anchovy. Allergens: egg, fish, milk, wheat.
Apple browns: toss it in lime juice. Allergens: tree nuts and egg.
Pineapple, mango, pawpaw, melon, orange, banana
Cooked chicken or tuna with mayonnaise, celery, onion
High risk: chill the chicken before mixing, keep at 5 °C or below.
Cooked, chilled shrimp on lettuce with Marie Rose sauce

flow: Wash and peel the potatoes; cut into even dice (about 2 cm) so they cook at the same time
Boil in salted water until just tender, so they keep their shape; drain
Boil the beetroot until tender; peel and dice (wear gloves; it stains)
Boil the eggs for about 10 minutes, cool in cold water and peel
Spread the potatoes and beetroot on trays and cool quickly; chill
Mix the chilled items with chopped onion, egg and mayonnaise, gently so the potatoes do not break up
Taste and season; cover, label and keep at 5 °C or below

blocks.note: Never mix mayonnaise into warm potatoes: the warmth encourages bacteria and makes the dressing oily. Never leave potato salad out on a warm buffet. It must stay on ice or in a chilled unit.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Green salads** are dressed **just before they are served**, because the acid and salt in a dressing make leaves wilt.
Use enough dressing to coat the leaves lightly, not to drown them. Serve extra dressing on the side.
Heavier salads, such as potato salad, are dressed when they are mixed, then chilled.

blocks.p: A **vinaigrette** is a simple dressing of oil and an acid (vinegar or lime juice) with salt, pepper and flavourings, and no egg. The usual proportion is **3 parts oil to 1 part vinegar**.

Whisk or shake the oil into the acid. It is a temporary mix, so it separates if it stands: shake it again before use. A little mustard or honey helps it hold together longer. Taste and adjust: add more acid if it is too oily, more oil if it is too sharp. Add salt, pepper, herbs, garlic, or a little scotch bonnet if wanted.
**Mayonnaise** is an **emulsion**: tiny droplets of oil held in a smooth, thick sauce by egg yolk. The yolk contains an emulsifier that holds oil and water together.

flow: Use pasteurised egg yolks, because the sauce is not cooked and raw eggs can carry Salmonella
Have all ingredients at a cool room temperature, and put the bowl on a damp cloth so it does not slip
Whisk the yolk with a little mustard, salt and a spoon of vinegar or lime juice
Add the oil **drop by drop** at first, whisking all the time, until the sauce starts to thicken
Then add the oil in a thin stream, whisking, until thick and glossy (about 200 to 250 ml of oil to one yolk)
Add lime juice or vinegar and seasoning to taste; cover, label and keep at 5 °C or below

ul: **Why does it split?** The oil was added too fast, or the ingredients were too cold or too warm. The oil droplets join together and the sauce turns thin and oily.
**To save a split mayonnaise:** put a fresh yolk (or a teaspoon of water or mustard) in a clean bowl and whisk the split mixture into it, a very little at a time.
Home-made mayonnaise is a high-risk food. Many kitchens use pasteurised yolks or ready-made mayonnaise. Keep it cold and use it within the time the plan allows.

head: Sauce
What it is
rows: Mayonnaise and tomato ketchup, with lime or lemon juice and a few drops of pepper sauce; for shrimp cocktail.
Mashed avocado (pear) with lime juice, onion and salt; use the same day, covered.
Yoghurt, herbs and garlic. Contains milk.
A light dressing for green and fruit salads. Egg-free and nut-free.
Hot sauce made from scotch bonnet. Serve on the side and warn guests.

blocks.note: Dressings with egg (mayonnaise, creamy Caesar) belong in the fridge and must be labelled. A buffet bowl of dressing needs to be on ice, like the salad.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Presenting a plated salad or appetiser

head: Point
What to do
rows: Clean, with no chips or cracks; the right size so the food is not crowded. Chill plates for cold food.
Mix colours: green leaves, red tomato, orange carrot, yellow pepper, pink shrimp. A single colour looks dull.
Pile food slightly in the centre, not spread flat.
Even cuts; leave space around the food; no spills.
Wipe the rim clean with a paper towel.
A small edible item that suits the dish; not too large; not on every plate by habit.
Right size, the same on every plate. Use a standard scoop, weight or count.
Cold food cold; hot appetisers hot.

ul: Choose a clean platter of the right size and line it with a doily or a bed of lettuce.
Arrange items in neat rows or a pattern, the same size and shape, with spaces between groups. Odd numbers look good.
Group by kind: all the fish canapés together, all the vegetarian ones together.
Do not overfill. Put a small garnish in the middle or at one end.
Keep spare platters in the fridge and replace platters rather than topping them up with old food.

blocks.h: Setting up and looking after a cold buffet

flow: Clean and sanitise the buffet table and equipment
Set up chilled display units, or trays of crushed ice, in good time so they are cold
Put food out as late as possible, in small or medium dishes, and keep the rest in the fridge to top up
Give every dish its own clean serving spoon or tongs, and a sneeze guard if the Centre uses one
Label every dish with the name and allergens
Check the temperature with a probe and record it; keep food at 5 °C or below
Replace dishes when they run low, rather than adding to old food; throw away food that has been out too long

ul: A tray of crushed ice under a bowl keeps seafood cocktail cold. Drain melted ice water often so it does not touch the food.
Keep hot food and cold food apart, and use a hot cupboard or chafing dish for hot appetisers (63 °C or above).
Do not let guests put used plates or fingers into the dishes.
Watch the buffet. A guest may reach into a dish with the wrong spoon.

blocks.note: In Jamaica's heat, even a short time outside the fridge matters. Take a small amount of food out at a time, and use ice and shade. Outdoor events by a pool or on a lawn need extra ice, covers against flies and a closer watch on the time.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Keep prepared salad items and toppings covered and labelled with the name, date and time, on the shelf above any raw meat or fish.
Store dry canapé bases in airtight containers so they stay crisp.
Do not dress or assemble until close to service.

flow: Store or throw away food as the label and plan say
Scrape, wash and rinse boards, knives and utensils
Sanitise with a food-safe sanitiser and air-dry
Wipe the benches and the fridge handles
Empty and wash the salad spinner and the waste bin
Wash your hands; report faults and low stock

blocks.note: Never mix bleach with other cleaners, because the mix can give off a poisonous gas. Follow the label and the Centre's rules.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: I can explain why salads and cold appetisers are high-risk foods.
I can describe good personal hygiene at the salad station, and why plasters should be blue.
I can handle ready-to-eat food with clean tongs or gloves and prevent cross-contamination.
I can name the temperatures for cold food, hot appetisers and cooked chicken.
I can take an allergy order and choose safe dishes for nut, egg, milk, fish, shellfish and gluten allergies, and vegetarians.
I can name the kinds of appetiser, and describe Jamaican ones such as Solomon Gundy, stamp and go and pepper shrimp.
I can name the parts of a canapé and say why the base is spread with butter or cream cheese.
I can work out how many canapés an event needs.
I can wash, dry, tear, cut and store salad ingredients.
I can explain simple and compound salads and the four parts of a plated salad.
I can make Jamaican potato salad, coleslaw, a green salad and a fruit salad safely.
I can make a vinaigrette in the right proportion and mayonnaise by hand, and fix a split one.
I can plate and garnish a salad or appetiser neatly, and arrange a platter.
I can set up a cold buffet on ice, label the dishes and know when to throw food away.
I can store prepared food, clean the station and report faults.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step: 'I dry the lettuce well, so the dressing sticks to the leaves and the salad does not go watery.'
blocks.label: Tip

c1.title: A wedding cocktail hour in Montego Bay
c1.text: A villa in Montego Bay is hosting 40 guests at a wedding cocktail hour. The caterer plans 3 cold and 2 hot pieces for each guest. The cold canapés are Solomon Gundy on crackers, callaloo and cream cheese on bammy rounds, and shrimp on cucumber slices, in equal numbers. The hot item is stamp and go. The cook wants to assemble everything three hours early and leave the platters on the counter.

c2.title: A salad buffet at a guest house in Mandeville
c2.text: For a family lunch at a guest house in Mandeville, trainee Tanisha mixes mayonnaise into potato salad while the diced potatoes are still steaming. She puts the salad in one big bowl on the buffet table in a warm room. After three hours the bowl is still on the table, half full, and the guests have finished eating.

c3.title: Dressings at a villa in Port Antonio
c3.text: At a villa in Port Antonio, Chef Gary makes mayonnaise by hand. He pours the oil in quickly, and the sauce turns thin and oily. He also needs 400 ml of vinaigrette at 3 parts oil to 1 part vinegar for the green salad. The villa's food safety plan says that raw egg must not be used in uncooked sauces.

c4.title: Special diets at a function in Kingston
c4.text: At a function in Kingston, one guest has a fish allergy and another is vegan. The menu offers a Caesar salad (made with a dressing that contains anchovy, and with parmesan and croutons), pepper shrimp, plantain chips fried in vegetable oil, crudités with guacamole, and callaloo and cream cheese on bammy. The same set of tongs is being used for the shrimp and the salad.

c5.title: The fruit and salad station in Ocho Rios
c5.text: At a hotel in Ocho Rios, trainee Kemar tosses a green salad in vinaigrette at 9:00 a.m. for a lunch at noon. By noon the leaves are limp and wet. He also cut the avocado for a salad an hour ago and the flesh has turned brown. He is about to slice a whole pineapple and a melon for fruit salad without washing them first, because he will peel them.

c6.title: A busy salad station
c6.text: Trainee Kerry-Ann starts a shift at the salad station with painted nails and a ring on her finger. Later, she wears disposable gloves to slice tomatoes, then takes out her phone to reply to a message, then goes on slicing with the same gloves.

questions.q: How many pieces of each cold canapé should be made?
questions.why: 3 cold pieces × 40 guests = 120 cold pieces, shared among three kinds = 40 of each. The hot item needs 2 × 40 = 80 pieces of stamp and go.

questions.q: Why is it wrong to assemble the cracker canapés three hours early?
o: The toppings lose their flavour while they wait in the fridge
The crackers go too hard if they are left to stand that long
The crackers go soggy and the toppings warm up
The guests will not know the food was freshly made for them
questions.why: Bases absorb moisture from the topping and go soggy. Assemble close to service, keep the toppings chilled and spread a barrier of butter or cream cheese on the base.

questions.q: Where should the shrimp on cucumber slices wait until the guests arrive?
o: On the counter, covered well with a sheet of cling film
In the freezer, so that they stay extra cold until service
In the fridge or on a tray of ice, at 5 °C or below
In a warm cupboard, to stop the cucumber slices sweating
questions.why: Shrimp is a high-risk food, eaten without more cooking. It must stay at 5 °C or below until service. Cling film on a counter does not keep it cold.

questions.q: Which allergen must be shown on the label for callaloo and cream cheese on bammy?
o: Egg
Milk
Peanuts
Wheat
questions.why: Cream cheese is made from milk. Bammy is made only from cassava, so it has no wheat, though a cook still checks the label. Label every canapé with its allergens.

questions.q: What was wrong with the way Tanisha mixed the potato salad?
o: She diced the potatoes, which makes them go soft and mushy
Mayonnaise went into warm potatoes, which need cooling first
She boiled the potatoes, which takes the flavour out of them
She mixed it in a large bowl, which warms the mayonnaise
questions.why: Warm potatoes warm the mayonnaise and make it oily. Warmth in a high-risk food also lets bacteria multiply. Cool and chill cooked items before mixing.

questions.q: What should be done with the half-full bowl after three hours?
o: Put it back in the fridge to be used for tomorrow's lunch
Throw it away if it is over the time the plan allows
Stir it well and leave it out for any guests who come late
Cover it and keep it on the table until the evening
questions.why: Cold food held out of the fridge beyond the time the plan allows (commonly 2 to 4 hours) may have grown dangerous levels of bacteria, even if it looks and smells fine. It cannot be saved by chilling or reheating.

questions.q: What is the best way to set up the potato salad on the buffet?
o: A small bowl on crushed ice, with the rest kept in the fridge
One big bowl at room temperature, with a lid on top
A big bowl beside the hot food, so the dish stays moving
A small bowl in the sun, so that the light shows off the colour
questions.why: Small amounts, kept cold on ice, with the rest in the fridge, keep potato salad at 5 °C or below. Replace the bowl with a fresh one rather than adding new salad to old.

questions.q: Why did Gary's mayonnaise turn thin and oily?
o: He used too much lime juice in the very first step
He whisked it for so long that the yolk broke down
He stood the bowl on a damp cloth, which cooled the yolk
He added the oil too fast for the yolk to hold it
questions.why: Oil is added drop by drop at first so the yolk can break it into tiny droplets. If it goes in too fast, the droplets join and the emulsion splits.

questions.q: What is the best way to make Gary's mayonnaise safe, following the villa's plan?
o: Use pasteurised egg yolks, or a ready-made mayonnaise
Add extra vinegar to kill the bacteria
Use only the eggs that are the freshest from the market
Whisk it for longer so the egg is cooked by friction
questions.why: Raw egg can carry Salmonella, and mayonnaise is not cooked. Pasteurised yolks have been heat-treated to make them safe. Vinegar or freshness does not remove the risk.

questions.q: How much oil and vinegar does Gary need for 400 ml of vinaigrette at 3 parts oil to 1 part vinegar?
o: 200 ml oil and 200 ml vinegar
133 ml oil and 267 ml vinegar
300 ml oil and 100 ml vinegar
350 ml oil and 50 ml vinegar
questions.why: 3 parts + 1 part = 4 parts. 400 ÷ 4 = 100 ml per part, so 300 ml oil and 100 ml vinegar. Check your sum by adding: 300 + 100 = 400.

questions.q: Which part of the Caesar salad is a risk for the guest with a fish allergy?
o: The cos lettuce, because it has a strong taste
The parmesan, because it is made from fish bones
The croutons, because they are fried in fish oil
The dressing, because it contains anchovy
questions.why: Classic Caesar dressing contains anchovy, which is fish, and fish can also be hidden in Worcestershire sauce. Read every label and tell the guest.

questions.q: Which items on the menu are suitable for the vegan guest?
o: Plantain chips and crudités with guacamole
Callaloo and cream cheese on bammy rounds
Caesar salad without the croutons on top
Pepper shrimp served without the pepper sauce
questions.why: Vegans avoid all animal products. Plantain chips fried in vegetable oil and crudités with a dip of avocado, lime and onion contain none. Cream cheese is milk; Caesar contains cheese and anchovy; shrimp is an animal.

questions.q: What is the problem with using the same tongs for the shrimp and the salad?
o: Traces of shellfish can reach the salad
The tongs will go cold and so spoil the shrimp quickly
The salad will take on the taste of pepper and shrimp
The tongs will be too heavy to lift the salad leaves
questions.why: Even a small trace of an allergen can be harmful. Every dish needs its own clean utensil, and an allergy meal needs clean equipment.

questions.q: Why were the leaves limp and wet by noon?
o: The vinaigrette had too little oil in it for the leaves
The leaves were washed in cold water before he used them
The salad stayed in the fridge until it was needed
The dressing went on three hours before it was served
questions.why: Acid and salt in a dressing make leaves wilt and release water. Dress a green salad just before it is served.

questions.q: What should Kemar do to slow the browning of cut avocado?
o: Leave it uncovered so that the air dries the surface
Squeeze lime juice on it, cover it and cut it late
Put it in a bowl of warm water until it is needed
Wrap it in a damp cloth and leave it on the counter
questions.why: Cut avocado reacts with air and browns. Acid from lime juice slows it, and covering keeps the air off. Cutting late is best.

questions.q: Why should the pineapple and melon be washed before they are peeled?
o: The skin is easier to peel when the whole fruit is wet
Washing the fruit makes the flesh taste a little sweeter
The juice runs more freely when the fruit is cold and wet
The knife carries germs from the skin to the flesh
questions.why: Soil and germs on the skin pass to the flesh on the knife as it cuts through. Wash and dry all fruit and vegetables, even those you will peel.

questions.q: What should Kerry-Ann do about her ring and painted nails before she handles salad?
o: Cover the ring with a glove and go on working as before
Remove the ring and keep off food with painted nails
Wash her hands twice and then carry on as normal
Put on two pairs of gloves to hide them both
questions.why: Rings hide dirt and can fall into food. Nail polish can chip off into food. Nails must be short, clean and unpolished, and rings (other than a plain band) removed. Gloves do not replace this.

questions.q: What should she do after touching her phone while wearing gloves?
o: Wipe the gloves on her apron and carry on slicing
Spray the gloves with sanitiser and carry on slicing
Carry on, since the gloves still look quite clean to her
Take the gloves off, wash her hands, put on new ones
questions.why: A phone carries germs, and the gloves now carry them to the food. Change gloves after touching a phone, face, bin or money, and wash hands before putting on a new pair.

questions.q: Why does salting shredded cabbage long before service make coleslaw watery?
o: Salt makes the cabbage swell and soak up the dressing
Salt breaks the mayonnaise down into oil and water
Salt draws water out of the cabbage, so mix it late
Salt makes the carrot release its sugar into the sauce
questions.why: Salt pulls water out of vegetable cells by osmosis, so the cabbage goes limp and the coleslaw becomes wet. Mix and dress it near service time.

questions.q: What must be done to cooked chicken before it is mixed into mayonnaise for a chicken salad?
o: Cool and chill it, so it goes into the mayonnaise cold
Leave it on the bench until it is just warm to the touch
Mix it while it is hot so that it soaks up the sauce
Rinse it in warm water so that it does not dry out
questions.why: Warm cooked chicken warms the mayonnaise and encourages bacteria to grow in a high-risk food. Cool it quickly, chill it, then mix, and keep the salad at 5 °C or below.
